mean: to slip up and give oneself away
lit: to let one's tail show, like a fox or tanuki in human disguise whose tail pokes out

use.how: Predicate with the deceiver or culprit as subject: 犯人がついに尻尾を出した. Often negative: なかなか尻尾を出さない. Only about hidden lies or wrongdoing.

near.diff: ぼろが出る is hidden weaknesses or ignorance showing; 尻尾を出す is a concealed lie or misdeed being given away by a slip.
尻尾をつかむ is said of the investigator who gets the proof; 尻尾を出す is said of the culprit who lets it slip.

cue: For months a cashier covered every trace of the missing money, until he carelessly mentions a figure only the thief could know.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]はとうとう{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: The culprit finally gave himself away.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]、怪[あや]しいよね。」「うん、でもなかなか{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]さない}んだ。」
ctx.en: "That guy is suspicious, isn't he?" "Yeah, but he never slips up."

ctx.en: If you keep piling up lies, sooner or later your story stops adding up and you give yourself away.

ctx.s: 経費[けいひ]を水増[みずま]ししていた社員[しゃいん]は、日付[ひづけ]の合[あ]わない領収書[りょうしゅうしょ]を提出[ていしゅつ]して{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: The employee who had been padding his expenses gave himself away by handing in a receipt with the wrong date.

ctx.en: The con man was cautious and never let anything slip in front of the police.

ctx.s: 刑事[けいじ]は、容疑者[ようぎしゃ]が{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]す}のをじっと待[ま]った。
ctx.en: The detective waited patiently for the suspect to give himself away.

bad.s: 初[はじ]めての発表[はっぴょう]で緊張[きんちょう]して、{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]して}しまった。
bad.en: (meant: I was nervous at my first presentation and made a mistake)
bad.why: It means a hidden lie or misdeed being exposed by a slip. An honest blunder is just a mistake (misu o shita, shippai shita).

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は正直[しょうじき]に{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]して}、自分[じぶん]のミスを認[みと]めた。
bad.en: (meant: she honestly owned up and admitted her mistake)
bad.why: It is an unintended slip, never a willing confession. To own up is to admit it honestly (shōjiki ni mitometa).

lit: to tuck one's tail between one's legs, like a dog that has lost a fight

use.how: Almost always 尻尾を巻いて逃げる, also 退散する or 撤退する. Mocks someone who backs off in fear before a stronger opponent.

near.diff: 逃げ腰 is a hesitant attitude of wanting to back out; 尻尾を巻く is actually fleeing, beaten or scared off.

cue: The loudmouth who has been challenging everyone at the bar sees the real champion walk in, and scurries out the back door.

ctx.en: "Are you going to turn tail and run just because they're strong?"

ctx.en: Overwhelmed by the champion's ferocity, the challenger slunk out of the ring.

bad.en: (meant: the players won the match and jumped for joy)

bad.en: (meant: the meeting dragged on, so I quietly left early)

mean: to find proof of someone's wrongdoing
lit: to grab the tail of a disguised fox, proving what it really is

use.how: The investigator is the subject: 警察が犯人の尻尾をつかんだ. Often potential negative: なかなか尻尾がつかめない.

near.diff: 尻尾を出す is the culprit's slip; 尻尾をつかむ is the other side, the one who catches it and gets the proof.

bad.en: (meant: after the teacher's explanation I finally got a handle on the problem)

bad.s: 犯人[はんにん]はうっかり{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかんで}、捕[つか]まった。
bad.en: (meant: the culprit carelessly gave himself away and was caught)
bad.why: The one who grabs the tail is the investigator. A culprit who slips up shows his tail (shippo o dasu).

mean: (of a wife) to boss her husband around
lit: to sit on someone as if he were a floor cushion

use.how: Wife as subject: 妻が夫を尻に敷く, or very often the husband in the passive: 奥さんの尻に敷かれている. Light teasing, not a serious charge.

near.diff: かかあ天下 is a noun for a household where the wife rules; 尻に敷く is the verb for her doing it, usually in the passive.

bad.en: (meant: my father is domineering and bosses my mother around)

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]を{尻[しり]に敷[し]いて}、無理[むり]な残業[ざんぎょう]をさせている。
bad.en: (meant: the manager pushes his staff around and makes them work unreasonable overtime)

mean: to take a lesson firmly to heart
lit: to engrave something on one's liver, the organ once seen as the seat of the spirit

near.diff: 心に刻む keeps a moving memory or words close to one's heart; 肝に銘じる fixes a lesson or warning so as to act on it.

bad.en: (meant: I made a note of tomorrow's meeting time in my planner)

lit: one's liver, the seat of courage, sits firmly in place and will not be shaken

mean: to astound, to take someone's breath away

mean: to frown in disapproval of others' conduct

ctx.en: Standing at my old teacher's grave, I naturally felt a sense of solemn respect.

ctx.s: 不祥事[ふしょうじ]が続[つづ]いたこの会社[かいしゃ]は、社員[しゃいん]全員[ぜんいん]が{襟[えり]を正[ただ]す}必要[ひつよう]がある。

r: さいふのひもをしめる
lit: to pull tight the drawstring of a pouch-style purse so no money gets out

use.how: Predicate with a person, household or consumers as subject, for a deliberate cutback: 今月は財布の紐を締めよう. Common in economic news about consumers.

near.diff: 財布の紐が固い describes someone who is habitually careful or tight with money; 財布の紐を締める is a deliberate cutback for a reason.

cue: Your rent just went up and your hours were cut, so you stop eating out and cancel two subscriptions.

ctx.en: I've got a trip next month, so I'd better cut back on spending this month.

ctx.en: "I heard your bonus got cut?" "Yeah, I'll have to tighten my belt for a while."

bad.en: (meant: it was a sale, so I loosened up and bought far too much)
bad.why: Tightening is cutting back, the opposite of splurging. When you spend freely the strings come loose (himo ga yurumu).
